Floating-point addition is not associative because modern hardware represents real numbers with finite precision. In exact arithmetic, the expressions (a + b) + c and a + (b + c) always have the same value. In floating-point arithmetic, however, each intermediate result is usually rounded to the nearest representable number according to a format such as IEEE 754 binary32 or binary64. Changing the grouping changes the intermediate values that are rounded, so it can change the final result.

The effect is especially visible when numbers have very different magnitudes. If a very small number is added to a much larger one, the small contribution may fall below the precision available near the larger value and disappear during rounding. If several small numbers are added together first, their accumulated value may become large enough to affect the result when it is later added to the large number. Cancellation can also magnify the issue: subtracting or adding nearly opposite values can remove leading significant digits, making earlier rounding errors more important. Overflow, underflow, subnormal handling, and the use of fused multiply-add instructions can introduce further hardware- and configuration-dependent differences.

Matrix multiplication relies on many dot products. Each output entry is a sum of products, and a large multiplication may require thousands or millions of terms per entry. Mathematically, those terms may be summed in any order. Computational systems exploit this freedom through vector instructions, cache tiling, multithreading, GPU thread blocks, and distributed reductions. A sequential implementation may accumulate terms from left to right, while a parallel implementation may form partial sums and combine them using a tree. Different thread schedules, tile sizes, processor counts, compiler optimizations, or libraries can therefore produce different reduction orders.

Because floating-point addition is not associative, these mathematically equivalent orders need not produce bit-for-bit identical matrix entries. Each difference is often tiny, but rounding errors can accumulate, and ill-conditioned calculations may amplify them. Consequently, rerunning a large matrix multiplication on another device, with another number of threads, or with a different library may yield slightly different results even when the inputs are identical.

Reproducibility requires controlling the arithmetic and reduction order. Implementations may use deterministic reduction trees, fixed scheduling, higher-precision accumulators, compensated summation, or specialized reproducible algorithms. These techniques generally cost performance, memory, or both. In ordinary numerical work, results are therefore compared using error tolerances rather than exact equality, while applications requiring bitwise reproducibility must explicitly choose algorithms and execution settings that guarantee it.
